slides.texte_overlay:
7 japanese habits that
quietly destroy laziness

Hara hachi bu. Stop eating when you're about 80 percent full. It's an old habit from Okinawa, and it kills that heavy, sleepy feeling after lunch that ruins the afternoon you planned to be productive.
Shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing. Twenty minutes walking among trees, no phone, no goal. Japanese studies link it to lower stress. Your head clears, and the drive you couldn't find indoors comes back.
Hansei. Every evening, ask yourself one honest question. "What could I have done better today?" No beating yourself up. Just one small fix for tomorrow, every single day. It adds up fast.
Shoshin, the beginner's mind. Learn something you know nothing about. Five minutes a day of history, art or science. Staying curious is the opposite of lazy, and it keeps your brain switched on.
slides.texte_sophia: Shoshin, the beginner's mind. A micro-learning app like the Sophia app gives you five minutes a day of history, art or science. Staying curious is the opposite of lazy, and it keeps you sharp.

slides.texte_overlay: Shokunin. Take pride in doing one thing really well, even the boring task. Do it the way a craftsman would. When you care about the quality, you stop looking for ways to get out of the work.

Kakeibo. Write every expense in a little notebook and review it at the end of the month. Seeing where your money really goes is the fastest way to stop wasting it, and it takes a few minutes each evening.
Ichigo ichie. One time, one meeting. Treat every moment like it won't happen again. It's hard to waste a whole evening on the couch when you remember today is a day you'll never get back.
